Soccer is a game characterized by sparse rewards, where even losing by a single goal can be considered a defeat. Consequently, scoring and preventing goals represent the most pivotal actions in a match. Leveraging the sparse reward structures inherent to real-time strategic decisions, we employ deep deterministic actor-critic learning to derive optimal policies for soccer. In this study, we incorporate time-dependent and goal-dependent state information, alongside contextual factors, to ensure the derived actions are contextually appropriate and optimized. Specifically, we encode contextual details by analyzing a soccer player's role and the elapsed time, while constructing soccer-specific (state) vectors that include player positions, the score difference, and possession status. The resulting policy outputs a combination of six distinct actions tailored to any given game state. To account for time-dependent variables, we utilize an attention-based mechanism to process soccer-specific sequences. Furthermore, we integrate tree-structured LSTM (TLstm) networks to capture dependencies within the soccer's state components. Ultimately, a neural network produces the final optimal action for each state. Validating our approach, we deployed it in a simulated soccer environment and compared the outcomes against a baseline method. Our findings indicate that integrating time and state dependencies significantly enhances performance; specifically, the attention mechanism improved performance by 7.5%, while the TLstm network added a 3.5% boost. Overall, our method achieved a 10.5% greater performance than the baseline. Additionally, our approach yields a policy capable of determining the most effective action for any specific game state. Our implementation is accessible at https://github.com/AbdulWahed/Context-Dependent- soccer- Attention-TLstm. Notably, the techniques described in this paper can be applied to other contexts involving sequential and contextual dependencies. For instance, in medical diagnostics, identifying the most suitable treatment for a patient relies on understanding the progression and interconnections of their symptoms. Similarly, in legal judgments, court rulings often depend on prior statements or evidence presented during a trial. These applications highlight the relevance of our contextual sequential framework beyond soccer simulations. By integrating attention mechanisms with TLstm networks, our method surpasses previous approaches in processing sequential data, offering significant advantages for real-time soccer simulations and related domains. Future work will focus on further optimizing this framework and exploring additional applications, such as medical and legal scenarios. Moreover, we aim to investigate the individual contributions of attention mechanisms versus TCPe and TLstm networks within this context-dependent architecture.

At colliders, neutral long-lived particles are identified either via displaced decay products or as missing energy, with the optimal search strategy depending on both the detector characteristics and the particle's decay length. This study examines the complementary nature of these signatures for the Belle II experiment, specifically focusing on axion-like particles ($a$) generated from meson decays. We introduce a novel approach to detect two-body decays characterized by $B^+ \to K^+ a$ followed by $a\to E\!\!\!/$, where $E\!\!\!/$ represents missing energy. Utilizing an integrated luminosity of $50\,$ab$^{-1}$, Belle II is capable of probing light invisible resonances with branching ratios $\mathcal{B}(B^+\to K^+ a) \gtrsim 10^{-7}$ and decay lengths $c\tau_a \gtrsim 1\,$m. For axion-like particles, we anticipate that the sensitivity of the $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ channel to small couplings could improve by up to two orders of magnitude relative to prior searches at fixed-target and collider facilities. Specifically, for sub-GeV particles, the combination of $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ at Belle II and beam-dump experiments offers the greatest sensitivity, whereas for heavier particles, the smallest couplings can be probed through displaced vertex searches at Belle II, long-lived particle studies at the LHC, and future fixed-target experiments. We provide simplified limits on axion-like particles from a comprehensive global analysis and project potential sensitivities for Belle II and upcoming facilities. Furthermore, we outline the requirements for future experiments needed to explore the "island of stability," a region of parameter space relevant to dark matter thermodynamics that remains unexplored by current or proposed experiments. To facilitate this global analysis, we have developed a public simplified model implementation available at \url{https://doi.org/10.21482/A.4.760}.
This paper offers a qualitative examination of potentially flawed outputs generated by contextualized embedding-based techniques for identifying diachronic semantic change. We first introduce an ensemble method that surpasses prior contextualized approaches, which then serves as the foundation for a detailed analysis of predicted semantic shifts in English vocabulary over five decades. Our results indicate that these methods frequently assign high change scores to words that are not actually undergoing genuine diachronic semantic shifts, or where the validity of such shifts is dubious. We provide detailed discussions of these challenging instances with specific examples and propose corresponding linguistic classifications. Ultimately, we conclude that pre-trained contextualized language models tend to conflate changes in lexicographic senses with variations in contextual salience, a bias inherent to their nature as distributed representations conditioned on local substrings. Finally, we suggest several potential directions for future research. Our study demonstrates that these advanced methods still encounter significant difficulties in accurately automating the detection of diachronic semantic change, a task historically central to linguistic inquiry. Furthermore, our detailed examinations of problematic cases yield insightful observations about English vocabulary that may prove valuable for future linguistic investigations. By integrating these findings with those from quantitative studies, researchers can develop more robust methods for diachronic semantic change detection, ultimately producing more precise embeddings aimed at automating lexicographic extraction. Such advancements could significantly benefit computational linguistics, natural language processing, and artificial intelligence. Additionally, our analysis of English vocabulary variations across time periods holds relevance for applications in language teaching and learning, as well as for linguistic research into vocabulary evolution.

Among the most critical hyperparameters for neural networks, the loss function plays a pivotal role, yet selecting the appropriate one remains challenging due to the vast array of available options. Despite this, related studies often fail to provide rigorous justifications for their specific choices, suggesting a dogmatic approach within the deep learning community that lacks empirical grounding. This work investigates supervised classification tasks to evaluate how loss function selection influences training outcomes. Although some functions yield suboptimal results, our empirical analysis demonstrates that underutilized losses, such as KL Divergence, can significantly surpass state-of-the-art alternatives. These findings underscore the necessity of treating the loss function as a tunable hyperparameter rather than adopting it as a fixed default. To facilitate this, we introduce NEURAL LOSS FUNCTION TUNING (NeuralLIFT), a module integrated into FastAI for easy hyperparameter optimization. Furthermore, we propose a new metric, NEURAL LOSS FUNCTION IMPORTANCE (NeuralLFI), designed to quantify the significance of the loss function during training; this metric serves as a guide for further tuning efforts. All source code, configurations, and pre-trained models required to replicate our evaluation and utilize NeuralLIFT are publicly accessible at https://github.com/AlexandreGuillouT/RETOC. We introduce ATOMIC, a comprehensive atlas of everyday commonsense reasoning structured through 877,000 textual descriptions of inferential knowledge. Unlike existing resources that primarily focus on taxonomic information, ATOMIC emphasizes inferential knowledge formatted as typed if-then relations involving variables (for instance, "if X pays Y a compliment, then Y will likely return the compliment"). To differentiate between causes and effects, agents and themes, voluntary versus involuntary events, and actions versus mental states, we define nine distinct if-then relation types. By generatively training neural models on the rich inferential knowledge within ATOMIC, we demonstrate that these models can acquire basic commonsense abilities and reason about unseen events. Furthermore, experimental findings indicate that multitask models utilizing the hierarchical structure of these if-then relation types achieve more accurate inference than those trained in isolation, a result confirmed by both automated metrics and human evaluation. Finally, we show that multitask models leveraging if-then knowledge graphs can acquire generative capabilities—such as answering questions and captioning images—without explicit end-to-end training for these tasks, a finding validated by automated measures, human assessment, and neural analysis. Ultimately, the availability of an resource like ATOMIC enables the systematic exploration of how humans connect events via simple if-then inferences, a capability essential for enabling neural systems to reason about unseen occurrences and engage in basic commonsense reasoning.

Hypothesis testing is a fundamental component of cognitive science, with Bayes factors offering a primary method for evaluating hypotheses based on their compatibility with observed data to facilitate selection among competing models. Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical application remains uncertain regarding the magnitude of effects required for distinguishing between Bayes factors that support different conclusions. This study examines the relationship between effect sizes and Bayes factors across four Bayesian statistical tests commonly used in cognitive science: the t-test, analysis of variance, effect size confidence intervals, and proportion confidence intervals. The analysis demonstrates that small effect sizes can yield Bayes factors favoring neutral hypotheses over those implying large effects. Simulated experiments indicate that this tendency persists with increased sample sizes. These findings suggest that researchers should anticipate Bayes factors supporting hypotheses with effect sizes comparable to those actually present in the data. Consequently, R. Hoekstra's (2014) recommendation for using a scale of "weakly supported neutral hypotheses" may be problematic, as such Bayes factors could reflect effect sizes similar to those in the dataset, merely indicating insufficient evidence for larger effects. Instead, this paper advocates for a more cautious interpretation of Bayes factors aligned with the data-centric philosophy of statistical inference promoted by G. Casella and L. Wasserman (1996). Additionally, the research highlights the utility of effect size confidence intervals as a complementary metric for evidence evaluation. Finally, the study concludes by proposing an updated hierarchy for evidence strength that integrates both Bayes factors and effect size confidence intervals. As demonstrated by recent work from J. Rouder and colleagues (2015), this dual-metric approach can identify stronger evidence for larger effect sizes even when Bayes factors remain low; for instance, an experiment might yield a Bayes factor of 3 in favor of a larger effect size, yet a 95% confidence interval for the effect size ranging from 0.1 to 0.5 would still suggest that the true effect size is more likely to exceed 0.05.
Discourse markers, such as {\it by contrast} and {\it happily}, are words or phrases that indicate semantic and/or pragmatic connections between clauses or sentences. Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). These inferences enable us to examine the relationship between discourse markers and the semantic relations annotated in these datasets. Although handcrafted mappings have been suggested between markers and discourse relations for limited sets of markers and categories, hundreds of discourse markers express a diverse range of relations, and there is no agreed-upon taxonomy of relations among competing theories (which are predominantly constructed top-down). By employing an automatic prediction method over existing semantically annotated datasets, we offer a bottom-up characterization of discourse markers in English. The resulting dataset, called DiscSense, is publicly accessible. Empirical evidence from this dataset supports a one-to-one correspondence between discourse markers and semantic relations, contradicting the view that multiple markers can signify the same relation. Furthermore, the data supports a one-to-one correspondence between discourse relations and Pragmatics of Sentence Pairs (PSP) categories, suggesting that current top-down theories may rely on an insufficient set of relations. Finally, our dataset supports a many-to-one mapping between discourse markers and functions (as defined in \cite{functions}), challenging the assumption that functions are inherently markerless categories. To facilitate further research, DiscSense is available at \url{http://vita.sif.it/discsense/}.

We present an implementation of a deep learning framework designed to explore dark matter structure formation. Specifically, we examine how velocity and density field data influence the construction of the halo mass function using cosmological $N$-body simulations. Our approach involves training a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on the initial snapshots of a dark matter-only simulation to forecast the halo mass into which individual particles will collapse by $z=0$, within the range $10.5 < \log(M / M_{\odot}) < 14$. Our findings indicate that incorporating velocity alongside density information yields negligible improvements when utilizing simulations based on the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model with an initial scalar perturbation amplitude of $A_s = 2\times10^{-9}$. To analyze ellipsoidal collapse models and assess velocity effects in smaller mass regimes, we increased the initial power spectrum. This adjustment allowed us to observe velocity impacts on larger halos that fall within our simulation's resolution. Consequently, the CNN model trained on simulations with a higher $A_s$ demonstrated significant improvements in halo mass prediction when velocity field data were included. Ultimately, for simulations where $A_s = 8 \times 10^{-8}$, the model relying solely on density information exhibited at least an $80\%$ increase in mean squared error compared to the model utilizing both velocity and density across nearly all mass scales, highlighting the failure of the density-only approach in this scenario. Our results conclude that the influence of velocity on halo collapse is scale-dependent, exerting a negligible effect under the standard cosmological model for mass scales between $10.5 < \log(M / M_{\odot}) < 14$. Furthermore, these implications are contingent upon the initial conditions of the universe. Detecting magnetic fields with high sensitivity remains a significant challenge in metrology. In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "test magnet"—via the Meissner effect. By combining this expulsion with the magnetic attraction between the superconductor and the levitating test mass, the magnetic field at the mass's location can be inferred from an atomic interferometric signal, even if the actual field is beyond the sensor's direct detection range. Leveraging the high precision of atomic interferometry, this method enables detection of fields that are too weak to be observed directly. Employing this approach, we successfully measured the magnetic expulsion by a lead (Pb) disk and a Pb-coated aluminum cylinder. These experiments yielded lower bounds on the magnetic susceptibility of superconducting lead of $\chi_{sc} < -10^{11}$ (95% confidence interval) for the disk and $\chi_{sc} < -5\times10^{10}$ (95% confidence interval) for the coated cylinder. These results align with prior literature and imply that the attractive magnetic force between the levitating test mass and the superconductor can account for an apparent violation of the equivalence principle at the $10^{-12}$ level. Furthermore, the methodology detailed here offers a general framework for investigating the macroscopic properties of newly discovered superconducting materials. Additionally, this technique can be adapted to search for axion-like particles through their potential induction of the Meissner effect. Our findings indicate that existing limits on the magnetization of bulk matter induced by axion-like particle interactions are insufficient to constrain the decay of such particles into photons for masses exceeding $10^{-12}$ eV; more sensitive measurements are required to explore this parameter space.

We introduce a self-energy-based theoretical framework designed to examine the angular dependence of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states emerging from a $d$-wave magnetic impurity situated on a superconducting substrate. Using a specific model for the magnetic degree of freedom, we numerically solve the resulting non-linear integral equations. To address this, learning strategies that leverage unlabeled data, such as semi-supervised learning (SSL), are gaining prominence. However, the effectiveness of SSL heavily depends on assumptions regarding the data distribution in both labeled and unlabeled sets, making the construction of an efficient unlabeled dataset critical. Furthermore, recent research indicates that regularized SSL methods can overfit to labeled data when paired with a high-resolution, resolution-specific dataset. Consequently, this paper examines the impact of dataset resizing on regularized SSL performance. We conducted a comprehensive study by first collecting a large, diverse set of skin images, from which we created multiple subsets of varying sizes and resolutions. These subsets were integrated into a positive/negative two-classification dataset and a supervised classification dataset. These were then employed to test regularized SSL methods across different data configurations. Our experimental results demonstrate that resizing the unlabeled dataset can significantly enhance classification performance, with a seven-fold increase in accuracy observed when moving from a 100-times smaller to a seven-times larger dataset. Additionally, we identified that data augmentation techniques perform better on natural images than on medical images. Finally, we developed a pipeline utilizing a resolution-specific split, which, when applied to the ISIC 2019 dataset, achieved state-of-the-art results on a 9:1 supervised-to-unsupervised split. This study examines the coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino behavior, and dark matter properties within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a direct link between neutrino oscillation lengths and the dark matter mass. We pinpoint viable parameter regions that satisfy all known constraints, highlighting four distinct viable mechanisms for generating the "solar" mass scale. Our analysis reveals that the atmospheric scaling relation $\mu_2 \sim \sqrt{m_{\rm atm}}$ demands a nearly degenerate 2-loop mass term, a feature absent in earlier iterations of this model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the lower bound on the dark matter mass is loosely connected to the seesaw scale, potentially allowing for an unexpectedly light dark sector. To explore this, we conducted direct detection experiments across a broad spectrum of dark matter masses and interaction strengths, uncovering potential observable signals even when the dark matter mass exceeds 100~GeV. Finally, we investigated cosmic evolution, particularly the universe's thermal history, to assess the impact of a light dark matter on the effective number of relativistic species during the early universe. These cosmological constraints prove to be significant, ruling out approximately half of the parameter space below the 10~GeV limit. Overall, this comprehensive study underscores the ability of minimal scoto-seesaw models to satisfy diverse physical, astrophysical, and cosmological requirements. Notably, the direct detection of the dark sector remains crucial for fully characterizing the dark matter candidate.
